steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our software testing paper proposing LSH-ART, an adaptive random testing approach that uses approximate nearest neighbor search (locality-sensitive hashing) to cut ART's cost. Cover random testing and ART, the overhead of the select-test-from-candidates strategy and existing fixes, our approach, a contributions list, and the paper's organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Random Testing: importance and applications
- Criticism of RT and Adaptive Random Testing
- STFCS, FSCS-ART and RRT, and their overhead as a nearest-neighbor problem
- Existing enhancements: forgetting and precise NN
- Our approach: LSH-ART
- Evaluation, contributions, paper organization

  - motivated by clustering of failure regions (inputs identifying failures) (cite)

- STFCS
  - many strategies, multiple implementations (cite); best known: Select-Test-From-Candidates Strategy
  - next test from random candidates by evaluation of executed tests (cite); "best" candidate selected
  - FSCS (cite) and RRT (cite): FSCS picks farthest candidate; RRT distance above threshold
  - distance per candidate per executed test -> high overhead as executed tests grow
  - nearest executed neighbor for each candidate -> instance of Nearest Neighbor (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Software testing is a very important software quality assurance activity in the software development life-cycle. There are many software testing techniques, and one fundamental approach is Random Testing (RT), which just selects test cases randomly from the input domain (the set of all possible test inputs). RT is popular because it is usually easy to implement, it generates random test cases efficiently, and it can give a quantitative estimation of the reliability of software. RT has been applied widely to different software applications, such as: SQL database systems; embedded software systems; Java Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers; security assessment; and .NET error detection. Arcuri et al. pointed out that RT should be recommended as the first choice for testing in many practical software scenarios.

Even though it is popular, RT has been criticized because it generally uses little or none of the available information when generating test cases. For example, Myers et al. described RT as maybe the "least effective" testing approach. Many approaches have been proposed to improve RT fault detection, and one of the most popular is Adaptive Random Testing (ART). ART is a family of enhanced RT methods that are motivated by the observation that failure regions (regions of test inputs that can identify software failures) are clustered. ART tries to spread random test cases evenly over the input domain, which may give better test case diversity than RT. Previous studies showed that ART is more effective than RT with respect to different evaluation criteria, like: the number of test cases needed to detect the first failure (F-measure); code coverage; and test case distribution.

Many different strategies have been used for ART, which has led to multiple ART implementations, and the most well-known and widely used one is the Select-Test-From-Candidates Strategy (STFCS). STFCS picks the next test case from a set of random candidates according to some criteria or evaluation of the test cases that were already executed: Each random candidate is compared (in some way) with each executed test case, and the "best" candidate is selected as the next test case. Two basic (and popular) STFCS implementations are Fixed-Size-Candidate-Set ART (FSCS) and Restricted Random Testing (RRT). FSCS-ART picks as the next test case the candidate that is farthest away from the executed test cases; RRT picks the next test case so that its distance from all the executed test cases is greater than a given threshold value. To generate each new test case, the distance between each candidate and each executed test case has to be calculated, which is a high computational overhead, especially when there are many executed test cases. STFCS needs to find the nearest executed test case for each candidate, as part of deciding which one is the "best" next test case. So a key part of STFCS can be seen as an instance of finding a Nearest Neighbor (NN).

- Existing enhancements to STFCS overhead
  - forgetting (cite): ignore some executed tests, fewer distances, sacrifices some fault detection
  - precise NN (cite): tree index such as k-dimensional tree, KD-tree (cite); still expensive in high dimensions or with many executed tests (cite)
- LSH-ART
  - Approximate Nearest Neighbor ART using Locality-Sensitive Hashing (cite)
  - uses all executed tests, retrieves approximate nearest neighbor -> lower search cost
- Evaluation: simulations + empirical studies, more than 30 real-life programs
- Contributions
  - first LSH-based approach for ART
  - framework, LSH-FSCS and LSH-RRT
  - comparable (sometimes better) effectiveness, esp. high dimensions
  - lower computational cost, esp. high dimensionality
  - more cost-effective than original ART in all scenarios, than variants in most
- Organization: Sections II to IX

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Software testing is a very important software quality assurance activity in the software development life-cycle. There are many software testing techniques, and one fundamental approach is Random Testing (RT), which just selects test cases randomly from the input domain (the set of all possible test inputs). RT is popular because it is usually easy to implement, it generates random test cases efficiently, and it can give a quantitative estimation of the reliability of software. RT has been applied widely to different software applications, such as: SQL database systems; embedded software systems; Java Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers; security assessment; and .NET error detection. Arcuri et al. pointed out that RT should be recommended as the first choice for testing in many practical software scenarios.

Even though it is popular, RT has been criticized because it generally uses little or none of the available information when generating test cases. For example, Myers et al. described RT as maybe the "least effective" testing approach. Many approaches have been proposed to improve RT fault detection, and one of the most popular is Adaptive Random Testing (ART). ART is a family of enhanced RT methods that are motivated by the observation that failure regions (regions of test inputs that can identify software failures) are clustered. ART tries to spread random test cases evenly over the input domain, which may give better test case diversity than RT. Previous studies showed that ART is more effective than RT with respect to different evaluation criteria, like: the number of test cases needed to detect the first failure (F-measure); code coverage; and test case distribution.

Many different strategies have been used for ART, which has led to multiple ART implementations, and the most well-known and widely used one is the Select-Test-From-Candidates Strategy (STFCS). STFCS picks the next test case from a set of random candidates according to some criteria or evaluation of the test cases that were already executed: Each random candidate is compared (in some way) with each executed test case, and the "best" candidate is selected as the next test case. Two basic (and popular) STFCS implementations are Fixed-Size-Candidate-Set ART (FSCS) and Restricted Random Testing (RRT). FSCS-ART picks as the next test case the candidate that is farthest away from the executed test cases; RRT picks the next test case so that its distance from all the executed test cases is greater than a given threshold value. To generate each new test case, the distance between each candidate and each executed test case has to be calculated, which is a high computational overhead, especially when there are many executed test cases. STFCS needs to find the nearest executed test case for each candidate, as part of deciding which one is the "best" next test case. So a key part of STFCS can be seen as an instance of finding a Nearest Neighbor (NN).

Different enhanced ART implementations have been proposed for the STFCS overhead problem, including forgetting and a precise NN approach. In the forgetting approach, some of the executed test cases are ignored ("forgotten") so that each candidate needs fewer distance computations. The precise NN approach instead often uses a tree-index structure (like a k-dimensional tree, KD-tree) to make the search faster. Forgetting does not use all the information of the executed test cases, so it can be seen as giving up some fault-detection capability. The precise NN approach still has to find the exact nearest neighbor for each candidate, and this can still be computationally expensive, especially if the input domain dimensionality is high or there are many executed test cases.

In this paper we propose an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) ART approach that uses the well-known ANN algorithm Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH): We call it LSH-ART. LSH-ART tries to balance testing effectiveness and efficiency. It uses all the executed test cases so that fault-detection performance is kept, but it retrieves the approximate (not exact) nearest neighbor of each candidate, which reduces the search cost.

To evaluate the approach, we ran a series of simulations and empirical studies with more than 30 real-life programs, and compared it with the original ART algorithms and their enhanced variants. The main contributions and findings of this paper are:

- As far as we know, this is the first paper proposing an LSH-based approach to improve ART performance.
- We propose a framework for LSH-ART, and give two implementations: LSH-FSCS and LSH-RRT.
- LSH-ART keeps testing effectiveness (including fault-detection effectiveness) comparable to the original ART and its variants, and sometimes it gets better results, especially for high dimensions.
- LSH-ART is more efficient in testing, and usually has lower computational costs (including for test-case generation) than the original ART and its variants, especially when the input domain dimensionality is high.
- LSH-ART is much more cost-effective than the original ART in all scenarios, and it is better than the variants in most scenarios.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section II gives some background information. Section III introduces our approach, with a motivating example, the framework, algorithms and complexity analyses. Section IV explains the experimental set-up used to examine the performance of the approach. Section V presents and analyzes the experimental results, and looks at some potential threats to validity. Section VI looks at extending our method from numerical to non-numerical domains. Section VII discusses software failures and faults. Section VIII discusses related work on ART. Section IX concludes the paper and gives some potential future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Software testing is an essential software quality assurance activity in the software development life-cycle [1,2]. Among the many software testing techniques, one fundamental approach is Random Testing (RT) [3], which simply selects test cases randomly from the input domain (the set of all possible test inputs). RT is popular due to its usual ease of implementation, its efficient generation of random test cases, and its ability to provide a quantitative estimation of software reliability [4]. RT has been widely applied to different software applications, including: SQL database systems [5,6]; embedded software systems [7]; Java Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers [8]; security assessment [9]; and .NET error detection [10]. As Arcuri et al. [11] have pointed out, RT should be recommended as the first choice for testing many practical software scenarios.

Despite its popularity, RT has been criticized for generally using little, or none, of the available information to support its test-case generation. Myers et al. [12], for example, described RT as perhaps the "least effective" testing approach. Many approaches have been proposed to enhance RT fault detection, one of the most popular being Adaptive Random Testing (ART) [13,14]. ART is a family of enhanced RT methods motivated by observations of clustering of failure regions (regions of test inputs that can identify software failures) [15,16,17,18,19]. ART aims to achieve an even spread of random test cases over the input domain, which may deliver better test case diversity than RT [20]. Previous studies [14] have shown ART to be more effective than RT in terms of various evaluation criteria, including: the number of test cases required to detect the first failure (F-measure) [21]; code coverage [22]; and test case distribution [23].

Many different strategies have been adopted for ART, resulting in multiple ART implementations [14], the most well-known and widely used of which is the Select-Test-From-Candidates Strategy (STFCS). STFCS chooses the next test case from a set of random candidates based on some criteria or evaluation of the previously-executed test cases [14]: Each random candidate is compared (in some way) with each previously-executed test case, and the "best" candidate is selected as the next test case. Two basic (and popular) STFCS implementations are Fixed-Size-Candidate-Set ART (FSCS) [13] and Restricted Random Testing (RRT) [24]. FSCS-ART chooses as the next test case the candidate farthest away from the already-executed test cases; RRT selects the next test case such that its distance from all previously-executed test cases exceeds a given threshold value. Generating each new test case requires calculating the distance between each candidate and each executed test case, a high computational overhead, especially when the number of executed test cases becomes large. As part of the decision process for choosing the "best" next test case, STFCS identifies the nearest neighboring executed test case for each candidate. A key part of STFCS can therefore be viewed as an instance of finding a Nearest Neighbor (NN) [25].

Various enhanced ART implementations have been proposed to address the STFCS overhead problem, including forgetting [26] and a precise NN approach [27]. The forgetting approach ignores ("forgets") some of the previously-executed test cases to reduce the number of distance computations for each candidate. The precise NN approach, in contrast, often uses a tree-index structure (such as a k-dimensional tree, KD-tree [28]) to speed up the search. Because forgetting does not use all the information of the already-executed test cases, it can be considered to sacrifice some fault-detection capability. The precise NN approach still needs to identify the exact nearest neighbor for each candidate, which can remain computationally expensive, especially when the input domain dimensionality is high or the number of executed test cases is large [25].

In this paper, we propose an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) ART approach using the well-known ANN algorithm Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) [33], which we call LSH-ART. LSH-ART attempts to balance testing effectiveness and efficiency: it makes use of all previously-executed test cases to maintain fault-detection performance, but retrieves the approximate (not exact) nearest neighbor of each candidate, thus reducing the search cost.

To evaluate our approach, we conducted a series of simulations and empirical studies with more than 30 real-life programs, comparing it with the original ART algorithms and their corresponding enhanced variants. The main contributions and findings of this paper are:

- To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper proposing an LSH-based approach to enhance ART performance.
- We propose a framework to support LSH-ART, and present two implementations: LSH-FSCS and LSH-RRT.
- LSH-ART maintains testing effectiveness (including fault-detection effectiveness) comparable to the original ART and its variants, sometimes obtaining better results, especially for high dimensions.
- LSH-ART has better testing efficiency, generally incurring lower computational costs (including for test-case generation) than the original ART and its variants, especially when the input domain dimensionality is high.
- LSH-ART is much more cost-effective than the original ART in all scenarios, and outperforms the variants in most scenarios.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II presents background information. Section III introduces the proposed approach, including a motivating example, the framework, algorithms, and complexity analyses. Section IV explains the experimental set-up for examining the performance of our approach. Section V presents and analyzes the experimental results and examines potential threats to validity. Section VI explores extending our method from numerical to non-numerical domains. Section VII provides some discussion of software failures and faults. Section VIII discusses related work on ART. Section IX concludes the paper and identifies potential future work.
